title: Adapter and Facade
goal: By the end you can wrap an outside program in an adapter that keeps its types, codes and exceptions to itself, use Kotlin extension functions as light adapters for data, and put a multi-step order behind a facade that owns the order of the steps and the failure rules.
opening:
You arrive at a hotel in another country with a phone charger from home. The socket in the wall has the wrong shape, so you push a travel plug adapter into it. The socket stays the same, the charger stays the same, and the little block in between makes them fit. Downstairs, the reception desk does a different job. You ask for breakfast at seven and fresh towels, and the desk talks to the kitchen and to housekeeping for you.

The corner shop has both problems. Its warehouse runs an old program, bought years ago, that speaks in item numbers and two-digit codes. And placing one order takes several steps across several parts of the program. The easy trap is to let the old program's codes leak into every class, and to let every caller repeat the steps in its own slightly different order.

In the last lesson, we built our own objects. In this lesson, we'll fit someone else's: an adapter that keeps an old program's words to itself, Kotlin's extension functions as light adapters, and a facade, one front desk for a job with several steps. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A Kotlin adapter implements `fun interface Courier { fun book(address: String): String }` and calls an old client method that throws `IOException`, with no try/catch. What happens when the old client throws?
options: It doesn't compile: the `IOException` must be caught or declared
The `IOException` travels straight through the port to whoever called `book`
Kotlin wraps it in an `UndeclaredThrowableException`
The exception is swallowed and `book` returns an empty string
warmup.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the code compiles, and the client's `IOException` reaches the shop's code through a port that never mentioned it. In Java the same adapter wouldn't compile, because the port's method doesn't declare `IOException`. So in Kotlin, translating foreign errors at the edge is a habit you have to keep yourself. The first section's Try it shows both languages side by side.

sections.h: Ports and adapters: where the translation lives
sections.body:
Adapter and Facade both wrap something, and so do Decorator, Proxy and Bridge, which you'll meet in the next two lessons. Their structure looks much the same, so intent tells them apart:

| Pattern | Wraps | Offers | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adapter | one object you can't change | a different interface: yours | make it fit your port |
| Facade | several objects | a new, simpler interface | hide a sequence of calls |
| Decorator | one object | the same interface | add behavior (*Decorator and Proxy*, lesson 5 of this track) |
| Proxy | one object | the same interface | control access (lesson 5 of this track) |
| Bridge | an implementation you pick | your abstraction | vary two things separately (lesson 6 of this track) |

In a program built with **ports and adapters**, a layout often called hexagonal architecture, you see Adapter and Facade on one picture. The shop's own logic sits in the middle and talks only to ports: `Warehouse`, `OrderBook`, `Notifier`. Adapters sit on the edge, one for each outside system: the old warehouse program, a database, a mail server. The facade is the front door, where the website or the phone line makes one call. The figure shows the lab laid out this way.

That layout pays off twice. Switching warehouses means writing one new adapter, and nothing in the middle changes. And the middle can be tested with lambdas: `new OrderDesk((product, grams) -> new Reserved("H1"), orderBook, notifier)` needs no warehouse, no database and no mail server.

Domain-driven design, a well-known way of organizing business software, calls a thick layer of adapters an **anti-corruption layer**: the place where an outside system's model is translated into yours, so it never spreads. The shop's old warehouse program needs one. It answers every request with a two-digit code and a pipe (`|`), like a clerk who stopped speaking in full sentences years ago. `00|H4711` means "held, and here's the hold id", and `51|` means "out of stock". If you find `"51"` anywhere outside the adapter, the layer has a hole.

The lab is that layer in miniature. `WarehouseAdapter` keeps the old program's item numbers, kilograms and codes to itself, and `OrderDesk` lets the website place an order without knowing the steps.

**Keep foreign words at the edge. The middle speaks only your own.**

Check yourself. The shop replaces its warehouse, and the new program throws `TimeoutException` where the old one threw `WarehouseException`. In a program laid out this way, which files change? (Only the new warehouse adapter, which catches the new exception and returns the same `Unavailable`. The desk, the shop's logic and their tests don't change, because they never saw `WarehouseException` either.)

compare.title: An anti-corruption adapter for the courier's status messages

java.title: CourierUpdateAdapter.java

kotlin.title: CourierUpdateAdapter.kt

compare.note: The courier's system sends a short status message whenever a parcel's state changes, in the courier's words. The translation is the same in both languages: their strings in, a sealed event of our own out. Kotlin writes it as an extension on their type, so call sites read `update.toEvent()`. Java needs a static method on a holder class, so call sites read `CourierUpdateAdapter.toEvent(update)`, and in bytecode the two are the same static method. Both use a catch-all branch on purpose. The courier's message types are an open set you don't control, unlike your own sealed types, where a missing case should break the build. Code that uses `DeliveryEvent` then switches over it with no default. Neither language makes Adapter unnecessary; Kotlin just makes the data-mapping kind cheaper to write.

worked.title: Wrap a map service behind a port, then test without it

steps.say: The shop prices a delivery by distance: 2.00 plus 0.50 for every kilometer. Its pricer calls an outside map service directly. The service answers with text like `"dist=4.2km;eta=11min"` and throws a checked `RouteException`. Before reading on, list every detail of the map service that leaks into `priceCents`.

Four leaks: the `"SHOP"` name the service wants, its answer format, its checked exception, and its hard-wired address. Define the port in the shop's words first. It says nothing about text formats or vendors, and an empty answer means "no distance right now".

Now the adapter. Everything the map service knows lives here: how it wants places named, how it packs its answers, and which exception it throws. Why return empty instead of rethrowing on `RouteException`? Because the port promised "kilometers or nothing", and the pricer decides what nothing means.
Test the two halves separately. The pricer gets a lambda. The adapter gets a fake map service, a subclass of the client that returns a canned answer, which is how the lab tests its warehouse adapter.

lab.title: A warehouse adapter and an order desk
steps: Read `OldWarehouseSystem.java` (the old program you can't change), `Warehouse.java` (the shop's port) and `Units.java` (two helpers). They're given; don't edit them. Run the tests: all ten fail.

Write `WarehouseAdapter.reserve`. Call `old.hold` with `Units.itemNumber` and `Units.toKilos`, catch `WarehouseException` and return `Unavailable(e.getMessage())`, then split the answer on `|` and map the code with a `switch`.

Write `OrderDesk.place` as a `switch` over the `StockResult`. Reserved: write it in the order book, send the confirmation (catching a failing notifier), and return `Placed`. Refused: send the sorry note and return `Refused`. Unavailable: return `RetryLater`.
Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: `raw.split("\\|", -1)` splits on a real `|` and keeps the empty hold id in `"51|"`. The pipe must be escaped, because `split` takes a regular expression.

A `switch` over the sealed `StockResult` with `case StockResult.Reserved ok -> ...` needs no `default`: the compiler checks all three cases. In a switch expression, use `yield` to return a value from a block.
Wrap only the notifier call in try/catch. If the order book throws, let it travel up: a reserved order that isn't written down is a problem someone must see, not one to hide.

drill.title: An adapter from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. An outside `PostcodeClient` has `String lookup(String postcode) throws LookupException`, returning text like `"Mill Lane;OLD TOWN"`. Your port is `interface DistrictOf { Optional<String> district(String postcode); }` (in Kotlin, `fun interface DistrictOf { fun district(postcode: String): String? }`). Write the adapter so the client's exception never escapes, and an empty or malformed answer gives no district.

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: An adapter makes a class you can't change fit your port. It translates arguments on the way in, and answers and errors on the way out.

Keep an outside system's types, codes and exceptions inside its adapter. A `"51"` or a `WarehouseException` anywhere else is a leak. Java's checked exceptions stop an `IOException` from escaping a port that doesn't declare it; Kotlin compiles the same leak without a word.
For a one-method port, a lambda or a `fun interface` is the adapter. For data, a Kotlin extension such as `SupplierItem.toProduct()` is the light adapter; in Java it's a static method.
A facade gives callers one call for a job with several steps, and owns the order of the steps and what each failure means. Keep it to orchestration only.
In ports and adapters, the shop's logic talks only to ports, adapters on the edge translate, and the facade is the front door.
The limit: neither pattern makes an outside system reliable. An adapter can only translate the failures it knows about, and a facade only knows the steps it was written with.
closing:
We started in a hotel with a travel plug and a reception desk. In the shop, the plug became an adapter that keeps the old warehouse program's codes to itself. The desk became one call that reserves, writes down and tells the customer, in the right order.

Now look in your own code for an outside system's words outside its adapter: a status code compared as a string, or a library's exception caught far from the call that threw it. Each one is foreign voltage leaking past the plug.

Next, we'll wrap an object and keep its interface exactly as it is. What can a wrapper add when it doesn't change the shape at all?

quiz.q: The warehouse adapter catches `WarehouseException` and rethrows it wrapped in a `RuntimeException`. The order desk catches that and checks `getCause() instanceof WarehouseException` to decide whether to retry. What's wrong?
options: Nothing, since the exception is unchecked now
The foreign type still leaks: the desk depends on the old program, so replacing the warehouse breaks it
A `RuntimeException` can't wrap a checked exception
Retry decisions belong inside the old warehouse program
quiz.why: Wrapping changed the exception's type, not who depends on it. The desk still imports `WarehouseException`, so it's tied to this one warehouse program. Translate inside the adapter into your own result (`Unavailable`) or your own exception type that says whether a retry makes sense. A `RuntimeException` can wrap anything, so that option is simply false.

quiz.q: Which statement about an adapter written in Kotlin is true?
options: An `IOException` thrown inside it can pass through your port without any compile error
The compiler forces you to catch the old client's checked exceptions
Extension functions can implement your port interface
`fun interface` ports can't be implemented with a lambda
quiz.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so nothing stops the client's `IOException` from reaching callers of your port. Java would refuse to compile the same adapter. Extensions can't implement interfaces, and a `fun interface` exists precisely so that a lambda can implement it.

quiz.q: Three parts of the shop's program (the website, the phone line and the shop counter) each reserve stock, book a van, write the order book and send an email, each with slightly different failure handling. Which pattern fits?
options: Adapter
Decorator
Facade
Singleton
quiz.why: A facade puts the sequence and its failure rules in one place, and each caller makes one call. An adapter changes one object's interface, a decorator adds behavior behind the same interface, and a singleton is about how many instances exist, not about running steps in order.

quiz.q: Which is the best use of a Kotlin extension function as an adapter?
options: `fun OldWarehouseSystem.reserve(...)`, which callers use instead of a `Warehouse` port
A global `fun Any.toJson()` in a shared utils file
An extension that caches the supplier's rows in a top-level map
`fun SupplierItem.toProduct(): Product`, kept next to the code that talks to the supplier
quiz.why: Turning a supplier's row into your own type is pure data translation, which is what extensions are good at, and keeping it next to the supplier code keeps the supplier's model contained. An extension on the old program makes callers depend on that program and can't be swapped in a test. A global utils extension spreads everywhere, and caching in a top-level map is hidden shared state.

quiz.q: From *Factory Method and Abstract Factory*: the shop now has one adapter for Pedal Post's old client and one for Big Blue Vans'. Where should the choice between them live?
options: In each caller, with an `if` on the parcel's weight
In one factory, a `switch` or `when` over the courier with no default, passed into the desk
Inside the desk's `place`, as string checks on the address
In the adapters: each checks whether the parcel belongs to it
quiz.why: Choosing which product to make is a factory's job: one exhaustive `switch` or `when` over a sealed or enum `Courier`, so adding a courier is a compile error in one place. Spreading weight checks over callers or the desk copies the rule, and adapters checking ownership turns every call into a guessing game.

flashcards.back: Makes an object you can't change fit the interface (port) your code expects, translating arguments, answers and errors.
One that lets the outside system's types, codes or exceptions (a `WarehouseException`, the code "51") reach your own code.

flashcards.front: A Kotlin adapter calls a method that throws `IOException` and has no catch. Does it compile?
flashcards.back: Yes. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the `IOException` passes through your port silently. Java would refuse.

flashcards.front: What does a Kotlin extension function compile to?
flashcards.back: A static method whose first parameter is the receiver. `item.toProduct()` is `toProduct(item)` in bytecode.
The order of the steps in a job with several steps, and what a failure at each step means. Not math, codes or database queries.

flashcards.front: Can a Java record component be named `notify`?
flashcards.back: No: "illegal record component name". Its accessor would clash with `Object.notify()`. The same goes for `wait`, `hashCode`, `toString` and the other no-argument `Object` methods.

flashcards.front: Adapter vs Facade, one line each?
flashcards.back: Adapter: one object, given a different interface (yours). Facade: several objects behind one new, simpler interface.

terms.plain: A wrapper that makes an existing object fit the interface your code expects.
An interface in your own words that your core code depends on, such as `Warehouse`.
An exception the Java compiler makes you catch or declare, such as `IOException`. Kotlin has none.
The adapters where an outside system's model is translated into yours, so it never spreads into your code.
One simple entry point that runs a job with several steps across several parts of the program.
A Kotlin function called like a method on a type it doesn't belong to; a static method underneath.
A layout where core logic talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge connect each port to one outside system. Also called hexagonal architecture.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a new teammate why `WarehouseAdapter` returns `Unavailable` instead of letting `WarehouseException` through, and why `OrderDesk` ignores a failing confirmation email but not a failing order-book write.
explain_back.answer: The adapter is the only class allowed to know the old warehouse program. If `WarehouseException` escaped, every caller would import the old program's type and make decisions on its status codes, and replacing the warehouse would mean changing all of them. So the adapter turns it into our own result, `Unavailable`, and the desk turns that into `RetryLater`. In the desk, the order matters. Once the stock is reserved, the order must be written down, so if the order book fails, that's a problem someone must see, and it travels up. The confirmation email is a courtesy. A broken mail server shouldn't turn a placed order into an error the customer retries, which could reserve the stock twice.

deeper.body:
The JDK has adapters you use every day. `InputStreamReader` adapts a stream of bytes into a stream of characters; its Javadoc calls it a bridge from byte streams to character streams, which shows how loosely the pattern names get used. `Arrays.asList` adapts an array into a fixed-size `List` that writes through to the array. `Collections.enumeration` and `Enumeration.asIterator()` (Java 9) adapt between the old and new ways of walking through a collection.

The GoF book describes two kinds of adapter. An object adapter holds the foreign object and delegates to it, as in this lesson. A class adapter inherits from the foreign class and implements your interface at the same time. Java and Kotlin allow the second only when the foreign class is open to subclassing, and it's usually worse: your adapter inherits every public method of the foreign class, so callers can go around your translation. Prefer the object adapter.

Kotlin's `by` delegation (in *Decorator and Proxy*, lesson 5 of this track) can build an adapter that forwards most of an interface unchanged and overrides the few methods that need translating. That works when the two interfaces are almost the same, such as two versions of your own API. For an outside system with a different model, write the translation out; it's the part that deserves a careful review.

Facades and slow calls mix badly in one way. Suppose a facade starts a database transaction, a group of database changes that succeed or fail together, and then calls a slow outside system inside it. The transaction holds a database connection for as long as the outside system takes. With a pool of 20 connections and a courier service that takes 120 ms to answer, a busy afternoon runs out of connections. Call the slow system first, outside the transaction, then write to the database in a short one.
